title: Last Branch Standing: A Potentially Surprising, Occasionally Witty Journey Inside Today’s Supreme Court
gist: A review of Sarah Isgur's book on the U.S. Supreme Court argues the conventional '6-3 partisan split' framing is wrong; the Court actually divides into thirds along an institutionalism axis (precedent, consensus, concern for the Court's public standing) that cuts across ideology, and remains the only branch still operating roughly as the Constitution intended amid congressional abdication and executive overreach.

themes.theme: Rethinking the Supreme Court's internal divisions

insights.claim: The widely held view that today's Supreme Court is simply another political actor split 6-3 along partisan lines is wrong, according to Sarah Isgur's analysis.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Investors and analysts modeling Supreme Court outcomes on regulatory, antitrust, or executive-power cases should not rely on a simple 6-3 ideological heuristic; a more granular institutionalism axis better predicts individual votes.
insights.quote: Isgur convincingly demonstrates that the widely held view that today’s Court is simply another political actor split 6-3 along partisan lines is wrong.
insights.locator: paragraph on the Court's internal divisions

insights.claim: Individual Supreme Court justices' judicial philosophies are shaped by a combination of ideology and how much weight they give to the Court's own institutional interests — with high-institutionalism justices valuing precedent, broad coalition-building, and public perception of the Court.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Offers a two-axis (ideology x institutionalism) mental model for forecasting how individual justices will rule on high-stakes cases, more predictive than a simple left-right split.
insights.quote: A justice scoring high on institutionalism, for example, puts heavy importance on precedent, prefers that as many justices as possible join an opinion, and worries about how a decision will affect the public view of the Court.

insights.claim: Applying the institutionalism framework, the current Supreme Court divides into thirds: institutionalist Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh, and John Roberts operate distinctly from Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Clarence Thomas, while within the liberal bloc Elena Kagan's jurisprudence departs from the less institutionalist Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: A concrete voting-bloc map — three institutionalist swing votes (Barrett, Kavanaugh, Roberts) — is directly useful for predicting outcomes on contested regulatory and executive-power cases rather than assuming a monolithic conservative or liberal bloc.
insights.quote: Analyzed this way, the current court is more properly divided into thirds, with the institutionalist Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kava-naugh, and John Roberts, operating distinctly from Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Clarence Thomas. Even within the liberal camp, Justice Elena Kagan’s jurisprudence departs from that of the less institutionalist justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

themes.theme: The Court as the last functioning branch

insights.claim: Isgur argues that Congress has abdicated much of its assigned constitutional role and the U.S. executive branch has accrued excess powers, leaving the Supreme Court as the only branch of government still operating roughly as the Constitution intended.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Frames the judiciary as an increasingly load-bearing check on executive power amid legislative dysfunction — relevant to expectations of continued litigation-driven policy reversals under the current administration.
insights.quote: Congress has abdicated much of its assigned role, she argues, and the U.S. executive branch has accrued excess powers, but the Supreme Court is the only branch of government still operating roughly as the Constitution intended.
